sam: Quick nsys run I did to capture kernel fingerprint + KV-cache warmup behavior. Trying to see why the first 50 requests pick a different kernel path when batching ramps from 1->8.

sam: Command I used (bracketed capture around warmup + 30s steady):
```
nsys profile \
  --output=artifacts/nsys_rampup_kf 
  --trace=cuda,osrt,nvtx \
  --capture-range=bracketed \
  --capture-range-start=5s \
  --capture-range-end=35s \
  --sample=cpu:timer:1ms \
  --force-overwrite \
  --wait-exec 
  -- 
  ./bench_infer --model=redwood-l2 --batch-schedule=adaptive --load=steady
```

sam: Notes: bracketed so we include the 2s warmup then the 30s steady window. NVTX markers around model.load and kv.prefetch.

anika: Nice — did you capture KV cache hits/misses via nvtx spans or by tracing our in-process counters?

sam: nvtx spans + a tiny stats export every 5s to stdout (so nsys picks up both GPU timeline and CPU-side markers). The stdout JSON has kv.{hits,misses} counters.

jordan: What did the kernel timeline look like? any different memcpy vs compute kernels early on? :eyes:

sam: Early window shows a short burst of small-matrix GEMMs (~64x64) then a transition to larger matmuls after the KV warms up. There's a ~200ms gap where osrt shows kernel selection probing (likely trying different algo paths).

lee: That probing gap rings a bell — could be our kernel selector running heuristics on first batch sizes. Did you capture the per-kernel SM occupancy / block config in the trace?

sam: Yes — the trace includes kernel params. I saw two distinct kernel variants for attention: attention_small and attention_fused. Small uses fewer registers, lower occupancy but lower latency for short sequences. Fused has higher occupancy but wins once seq len or batch grows. The cutoff seemed to shift when kv cache warmed (i.e., sequence prefix changed).

anika: So KV cache warmup affects effective sequence lengths (more cached prefix => longer active seq downstream) and flips kernel choice? Makes sense. Any ideas to get deterministic kernel selection for first N requests so we avoid perf regressions in ramp-up?

sam: A few actionable items I noted in the trace: 
- Emit an NVTX marker at the exact iteration we want to bracket (we already did).
- Force a one-shot small-batch warmup before switching to adaptive batching (adds ~100ms but stabilizes kernel choice).
- Pin kernel selector seed/threshold in runtime during ramp-up.

jordan: For reproducing, can you paste the nvtx bracket snippet?

sam: Sure:
```c
NVTX_RANGE_PUSH("kv.prefetch");
// prefetch keys into host/GPU cache
kv->prefetch(prefix_keys);
NVTX_RANGE_POP();
NVTX_RANGE_PUSH("infer.iter");
run_iter();
NVTX_RANGE_POP();
```

lee: Perf-bot catches: did you run with OSRT sampling enabled? sometimes sample-based traces miss short kernels.

perf-bot: Automated note: capture artifacts uploaded to s3://redwood-perf/nsys/2912345678/. nsys export produced: timeline.svg (gpu kernels), nvtx_summary.txt, stdout-kv-stats.json.

anika: Good. One more: try switching sample to --sample=osrt:gpu-activity and increase capture duration to 45s to get more steady-state overlap — sometimes kernel handoffs happen at 20s mark.

sam: Agreed. I'll re-run with --capture-range-start=3s and end=48s and include a forced 5-iter small-batch warmup before enabling adaptive batching. Will post results.

jordan: If re-run shows selector flipping after kv hit-rate crosses ~0.6, let's add an explicit hysteresis in selector (require sustained metric for 3 consecutive windows).

lee: Also add a short README in the artifact dir describing the capture flags and the exact command used — saved me a lot last time.

sam: Will do. TL;DR: bracketed nsys + nvtx + stdout counters gave clear correlation: KV warmup -> effective seq growth -> kernel variant flip. Next steps: deterministic warmup + selector hysteresis + longer bracketed traces. :+1:
